narrative:
The model predicted a 56% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability tipped above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Three factors drove this outcome, ranked by importance. First, your decision to attend law school part-time rather than full-time was the strongest influence. The vast majority of accepted students (93%) planned to study full-time; your part-time status pushed the prediction noticeably toward failure. Second, your undergraduate GPA of 2.4 was well below the 3.23 average of accepted students and added further weight toward a likely bar exam failure. Third, your family income bracket of upper-middle actually worked slightly in your favor, nudging the prediction a little toward passing, but it was not enough to overcome the other two factors.

Taken together, the part-time schedule and lower grades created a picture of higher risk that the model could not ignore. Gender and race played no role in this decision.

To improve your chances, consider reapplying after strengthening your academic record—perhaps by raising your LSAT score or completing additional coursework that demonstrates stronger performance. Full-time enrollment, if feasible, would also remove the largest negative signal the model saw. Focus on those two areas, and you can materially change how future predictions view your application.
